text: 50-year-old male. The patient reports a progressively increasing swelling on the nape of his neck for 2 months. He denies having a fever, pain, or any discharge from the swelling. He mentions a history of colon cancer for which he underwent colectomy at the age of 43. He also has a history of type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, and osteoarthritis of the left knee. He takes insulin glargine, metformin, enalapril, and naproxen.

speaker: Doctor
text:
DIAGNOSIS READY: Metastatic Squamous Cell Carcinoma of the Head and Neck (specifically from the tonsillar base/oropharynx).

The patient's history of a painless, progressively enlarging cervical mass over two months, combined with a significant age (50) and risk factors for head and neck cancer (implied by the location and chronicity), makes this the most critical diagnosis to consider. The history of colon cancer is less likely to present as an isolated neck mass without systemic symptoms or other signs of recurrence, and the lack of pain or fever makes acute infection like an abscess unlikely. I will now confirm the diagnosis with imaging. REQUEST IMAGES: Neck Ultrasound and CT Neck.
